items.rawSummary: Iran has announced a full closure of the Strait of Hormuz and suspension of transit permits, while U.S. Central Command insists the waterway remains open and that hundreds of vessels have transited in recent months, as Japan draws on oil reserves and the U.S. Treasury plans to use frozen Iranian assets to offset transit tolls.
items.analysis: Iran announced a complete closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the immediate suspension of all transit permits, ordering vessels with existing permits to hold position and await instructions. The IRGC Navy stated the closure would continue due to repeated ceasefire violations by the American side and warned that any ship approaching the strait would be regarded as cooperating with the enemy, claiming it had struck two vessels that tried to transit. U.S. Central Command announced that the strait remains open, with hundreds of ships transiting in recent months, and denied any sea skirmishes or that any U.S. warships had been hit; President Trump disclosed that a previously secret U.S. mission had escorted over 200 ships and seized Iranian oil vessels. Japan has drawn down 36.5 million barrels of reserves and is buying roughly eight times more U.S. crude than a year ago to offset the disruption, while U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced plans to use frozen Iranian assets to pay for allied damage and offset any tolls Iran charges for Strait of Hormuz passage, opening a new financial dimension to the standoff.

U.S. Central Command announced that the strait remains open, with hundreds of ships transiting in recent months, and denied any sea skirmishes or that any U.S. warships had been hit; President Trump disclosed that a previously secret U.S. mission had escorted over 200 ships and seized Iranian oil vessels. Japan has drawn down 36.5 million barrels of reserves and is buying roughly eight times more U.S. crude than a year ago to offset the disruption, while U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced plans to use frozen Iranian assets to pay for allied damage and offset any tolls Iran charges for Strait of Hormuz passage, opening a new financial dimension to the standoff.

items.description: The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump plans to attack Iran every night until a deal is reached.
items.rawSummary: U.S. strikes on Iranian military targets have continued, and President Trump has escalated both the scale of promised attacks and the stated strategic objectives, including seizing oil infrastructure, while the U.S. military frames operations as self-defense.
items.analysis: U.S. strikes on Iran, which CENTCOM describes as self-defense against surveillance, communications, and air defense sites, persisted through June 10, with Tomahawk launches from the USS Michael Murphy. President Trump told Fox News that Iranian officials requested a halt, leading to a brief pause, but after no agreement emerged he announced a sharp escalation of objectives: he now says the U.S. will strike Iran 'very hard' tonight and will eventually seize Kharg Island and other oil infrastructure to control Iran's oil and gas markets. In subsequent remarks he characterized the coming strikes as 'bigger, bigger, more powerful' and suggested a small group of soldiers could take control, while the Wall Street Journal reported a plan to attack Iran nightly until a deal is reached. Trump has since reiterated that tonight's bombing will be 'bigger, more powerful,' confirming the imminent resumption. Iran's armed forces have vowed a forceful response, and oil prices have risen on the threat to infrastructure.
